prompt: A look at show 990 returned `Server-Timing: db;dur=10.2, pay;dur=0.0, total;dur=10.7`, and curl measured 11.461 ms in all. Where did the time go?
hint: Subtract each clock from the one outside it.

choices.text: Into the network between curl and the server
choices.why: curl's total and the server's total differ by under a millisecond; the network added almost nothing.

choices.text: Into the payment provider's 40 ms
choices.why: pay is 0.0: looking at a show pays nothing.

choices.text: Into the database query
choices.why: Right. 10.2 of the server's 10.7 ms, which is nearly all of curl's 11.461 too.

choices.text: Into Python starting a thread for the request
choices.why: That cost is inside the server's total but outside db, and the gap is only 0.5 ms.

prompt: A booking returned `Server-Timing: db;dur=15.7, pay;dur=40.1, total;dur=58.2`. How many milliseconds of it did no named part account for?
Match each observation from this lesson to the USE question it answers.
Under eight workers looking at shows, top's second snapshot showed `python3 app.py` at 212.5% and `python3 measure.py 8 12` at 6.5%. What does that pair of numbers rule out?
hint: Which of the two programs could be the limit?

choices.text: That the generator was what limited the test
choices.why: Right. The generator was nearly idle; the server's process was using more than two processors.

choices.text: That the database was slow
choices.why: SQLite runs inside the server's process, so its work is part of the 212.5%.

choices.text: That the machine was short of memory
choices.why: %CPU says nothing about memory; free and vmstat's si and so do.

choices.text: That a lock was involved anywhere in the server
choices.why: A lock can sit in a busy process too; this pair only says the server is the busy one.

prompt: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` printed `SCAN bookings` for the count of one show's bookings. What does SCAN tell you?
hint: Compare it with the SEARCH that followed the index.

choices.text: The query is wrong and returns too many rows
choices.why: The count was right; a scan is about cost, not correctness.

choices.text: It reads every row of the table
choices.why: Right. Every one of nearly three hundred thousand rows, on every request.

choices.text: The result is cached after the first request
choices.why: Nothing in the plan says so, and the timings did not fall on repeat.

choices.text: The table is locked while the count runs
choices.why: Readers do not lock each other out in SQLite; the lock in this lesson is app.py's own.

prompt: After the index, the plan said `USING COVERING INDEX bookings_by_show`. What does COVERING add to SEARCH?
hint: What does a count of rows for one show need to read?

choices.text: The table itself is not read at all
choices.why: Right. A count by show_id needs nothing but the show_id values the index already holds.

choices.text: The index covers every column of the bookings table
choices.why: It holds one column, show_id; it covers the query, not the table.

choices.text: Every show has at least one booking in it
choices.why: The word is about which data the query needs, not about the data's contents.

choices.text: The index is kept in memory and never written to disk
choices.why: An index is stored in the database file like the table.

prompt: In SQLite, prefixing a query with EXPLAIN QUERY ___ prints how it will be run, without running it.
What does the index on bookings(show_id) cost the box office?
hint: Think about what happens when a row is added.

choices.text: Nothing, since an index only ever speeds things up
choices.why: Indexes are paid for on every write and in disk space.

choices.text: Each booking writes an index entry as well as the row
choices.why: Right. Worth it on a table read far more than written; a load test of the writes says when it is not.

choices.text: Counts become approximate rather than exact
choices.why: An index changes how rows are found, never which rows exist.

choices.text: Two bookings for the same seat become impossible
choices.why: That is a unique index on (show_id, seat), the one app_fixed.py creates.

prompt: Every successful booking holds one global lock for at least its 40 ms payment. At most how many successful bookings can finish per second, whatever the load?
hint: One second divided by the time each holds the lock.

prompt: With sixteen workers booking, throughput was flat, the median was 401.2 ms, and top showed app.py at 10% of a processor. What kind of resource is the bottleneck?

choices.text: The processors, which are too slow for Python
choices.why: They were nearly idle; a busy processor shows up in %CPU.

choices.text: The disk, which every booking writes to
choices.why: Possible in general, but a disk-bound server shows wa rising; here the fix to the lock multiplied bookings.

choices.text: A software resource that requests queue for
choices.why: Right. Hardware idle, throughput flat, latency rising: a lock, a pool or a queue. Here, booking_lock.

choices.text: The generator, which cannot send faster
choices.why: measure.py was at a few percent; it was waiting for answers, not short of processor.

prompt: Put the steps app_fixed.py takes for a booking in order.
hint: The database decides the winner before anybody pays.
items: Read show_id, seat and customer from the request
Check that the seat exists in a show on sale
Insert the row and commit, or answer 409 if the unique index refuses it
Charge the customer, with no lock held
trap: Paying before the insert would charge the loser of a race for a seat it then cannot have.

prompt: Twenty threads booked seat 1 of show 990 at once against app_fixed.py and got one 201 and nineteen 409s. Which part of app_fixed.py made that outcome certain?

choices.text: The barrier in race.py, which sends the requests together
choices.why: The barrier makes the test hostile; it does nothing to protect the seat.

choices.text: disable_nagle_algorithm, which answers each request at once
choices.why: That changes when bytes leave the server, not who gets the seat.

choices.text: The unique index on show and seat
choices.why: Right. The database refuses a second row for the seat, whichever insert arrives second.

choices.text: The queue of 128 connections, which serves them in order
choices.why: The accept queue orders connections, not commits; twenty threads still run at once.

prompt: On app.py, every request after the first on one kept connection took about 44 ms at the client, while the server reported 0.3 ms for the second. What held the answer back?
hint: Two TCP rules, one on each side.

choices.text: Nagle's algorithm, waiting on the client's delayed ACK
choices.why: Right. The body waits for the headers to be acknowledged, and the client delays that acknowledgement by 40 ms.

choices.text: The database, which counts the bookings of a show on every request
choices.why: These were requests for /health, which runs no query.

choices.text: The 40 ms payment provider
choices.why: /health pays nothing; the match with 40 ms is a coincidence of two different constants.

choices.text: Opening a new connection for each request
choices.why: These requests reused one connection; the fresh connections were the fast ones.

prompt: A run with 32 workers on app.py had a median of 9.0 ms, a p99 of 1035.5 ms and 190 TcpExtListenOverflows. Where did the requests near one second spend that second?
hint: The application never saw them during it.

choices.text: Waiting for booking_lock
choices.why: That run only looked at shows; no booking took the lock.

choices.text: Before their connection was accepted, waiting to retry
choices.why: Right. The kernel dropped the opening packet while the accept queue of 5 was full, and the client retried a second later.

choices.text: In a slow database query
choices.why: With the index every query took a fraction of a millisecond.

choices.text: Inside measure.py, which could not keep up
choices.why: A generator at its limit sends less; it does not add a second to a request it timed.

prompt: After the accept queue was raised, 32 workers completed 626.2 requests a second. By Little's law, about what mean response time should the report show, in ms?
hint: Requests inside the system = throughput × time each spends there.

prompt: A tester runs a load generator on a laptop against a staging server in another country. The client sees 310 ms per request, Server-Timing says total 22 ms, and curl's time_connect is 145 ms. Where is most of the time?
hint: Subtract the server's clock from the client's, then read time_connect.

choices.text: In the database, which Server-Timing cannot see
choices.why: The database is inside the server's total of 22 ms.

choices.text: In the application, where the 22 ms are spent
choices.why: 22 of 310 ms is the smaller part; the gap is outside the server.

choices.text: In the network: about 145 ms each round trip, and a request needs two
choices.why: Right. One round trip to connect, one for the request: about 290 ms of the 310 before the server's 22.

choices.text: In the laptop's processors, which slow the generator
choices.why: A busy generator sends fewer requests; it does not make time_connect 145 ms.

prompt: A Python load generator shows one processor fully used by its own process, the server's process at 40%, and throughput flat as workers are added. What should the tester do next?
hint: Which of the two programs is at its ceiling?

choices.text: Report the flat throughput as the capacity of the server under test
choices.why: The flat line is the generator's ceiling; the server was never pushed to its own.

choices.text: Add a second generator and measure again
choices.why: Right. Or a more efficient one: until the generator has room, the test measures the generator.

choices.text: Add an index to the busiest query of the server
choices.why: The server is at 40%; nothing says the database limits anything yet.

choices.text: Raise the server's accept queue
choices.why: Dropped connections show as a tail near one second and a counter in nstat, neither of which is described.

prompt: Which of these can saturate while every processor, disk and network link on the machine looks idle? Choose every one that can.

choices.text: A lock held while calling a slow external service
choices.why: Yes. booking_lock did exactly that at 10% CPU.

choices.text: A pool of database connections smaller than the number of threads
choices.why: Yes. Threads wait for a free connection while nothing is busy.

choices.text: The kernel's queue of connections waiting to be accepted
choices.why: Yes. It overflowed at 5 while the server was answering in milliseconds.

choices.text: A scan of a table with no index
choices.why: A scan is work: it shows as processor time, as it did at 212.5%.

choices.text: A process swapping its memory to disk
choices.why: Swapping is the disk at work, and shows in si, so and wa.
